ethiopia.summary: On November 2, 2026, Ethiopia's Media Authority (EMA) indefinitely suspended the registration of Media and Communication Center PLC, which publishes the Amharic-language Reporter and the English-language The Reporter. This action raises significant concerns about accountability and transparency in media regulation. The EMA claims the suspension was due to the publisher's repeated dissemination of distorted and unverified information, but it has not provided specific examples or evidence to support these allegations. Critics, including Human Rights Watch and Reporters Without Borders, argue that the decision reflects a broader crackdown on independent journalism in Ethiopia, particularly following the publication of a critical editorial by The Reporter. The lack of transparency in the EMA's decision-making process undermines public confidence and raises questions about whether the suspension was politically motivated. To restore trust, the EMA must clarify its rationale, provide evidence for its claims, and ensure that media regulations are applied fairly and consistently across all outlets.

ethiopia.title: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: In-Depth Analysis - Emptied of Civilians, No End in Sight - How the Escalating Moyale Conflict Is Deepening a Humanitarian Crisis 18 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Once a bustling border town sustained by cross-border commerce, pastoralist livelihoods and closely interconnected communities, Moyale is increasingly being emptied of its civilian population as escalating clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces drive residents from their homes, disrupt economic activity and push tens of thousands across the border into Kenya. The latest escalation was reported on November 16, when fighting intensified throughout the day, leaving numerous residential homes and businesses burned, while thousands more people continued to flee. Residents who spoke to Addis Standard described a town where the sounds of children going to school and merchants arriving for business have largely disappeared, replaced by military deployments, exchanges of heavy gunfire and the fear of further displacement. Accounts provided to Addis Standard by displaced residents, refugees and a Kenyan Member of Parliament representing the Kenyan side of Moyale point to a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation. Families who have crossed into Kenya in search of safety are confronting shortages of food, milk, clean water and adequate shelter, while those who remain or have returned to protect their properties face continuing insecurity. The escalation comes a month after the conflict erupted on October 18, 2026, following territorial disputes over the hoisting of a Somali Regional State flag in Moyale and the fatal shooting of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa . Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn What began as a familiar confrontation in the dually administered border town, quickly degenerated into armed confrontation between Oromia and Somali regional forces. Fullend by intensive media narrative on both sides, the conflict has since evolved into a wider security and humanitarian crisis , with fighting spreading to neighboring districts into Borana Zone, southern Oromia, and its consequences increasingly felt across the Kenyan border. The scale of displacement reflects the growing severity of the crisis. Nearly 50,000 Ethiopians have fled into northern Kenya, particularly Marsabit County, while more than 10,000 Kenyan residents had also been displaced by the spillover violence. The continuing influx has placed additional pressure on host communities and local administrations already struggling to provide emergency assistance. For many displaced families, however, crossing the international boundary has offered neither lasting security nor relief from the consequences of the conflict. It is almost a month since we fled from Moyale, Kebele 02 (Bole). Yet, what we hear from the direction of our neighborhood is still not good news Kule Boru Kule Boru, a mother who fled from Kebele 02 (Bole) in Moyale town with her three children, all under the age of 10, told Addis Standard that nearly a month after leaving her home, she remains trapped in severe uncertainty and increasingly difficult living conditions. The absence of income in Kenya has made it difficult for her to provide for her children. Two of them are struggling with a lack of milk and adequate nutrition, while the others have been forced to discontinue their education. The family also lacks adequate shelter and assistance. "It is almost a month since we fled from Moyale, Kebele 02 (Bole). Yet, what we hear from the direction of our neighborhood is still not good news; every day we hear the sound of gunfire, homes burning, many people we know dying, and the few people who remained in their neighborhoods being displaced," Kule told Addis Standard . Further describing the difficulties confronting her family, she said: "Here in Kenya, we have no jobs at all. Two of my young children are suffering from a lack of milk; the others have been cut off from their education. The lack of suitable shelter and adequate assistance has put us under immense stress, and we live in constant worry about whether our house will be burned down today or tomorrow." Her experience reflects a broader humanitarian emergency among Ethiopian families displaced into Kenya. A November 10 report by Addis Standard found that food shortages were affecting 71% of Ethiopian displaced families in Kenyan Moyale. Local officials have appealed to UN agencies and humanitarian partners for emergency food, shelter, medical supplies, clean water and sanitation support. From the day the war started, we fled Moyale carrying our newborn baby who had just come into the world. At first, based on what we had seen in the past, we thought this war would last a week at most Abdi Edin The consequences are particularly acute for children, pregnant and postpartum women, and elderly people, whose vulnerability increases as displacement becomes prolonged and access to basic necessities deteriorates. Abdi Edin, a 25-year-old merchant from the Somali-administered side of Moyale, told Addis Standard that he had been forced to flee twice with his newborn baby and postpartum wife after fighting broke out. His wife had given birth only three weeks before the violence began, and the couple had been married for less than a year. Initially believing the fighting would subside within days, Abdi crossed into Kenya with his family and temporarily settled in Al-Huda. But the insecurity and humanitarian difficulties there soon forced them to move again. "From the day the war started, we fled Moyale carrying our newborn baby who had just come into the world. At first, based on what we had seen in the past, we thought this war would last a week at most; however, because the fighting did not stop, we temporarily settled on the Kenyan side at a place called Al-Huda," Abdi told Addis Standard . The family subsequently faced another displacement after heavy weapons fired from the Ethiopian side reportedly crossed into Kenyan territory, causing damage and further threatening civilians. "We faced many humanitarian challenges at Al-Huda. Furthermore, when heavy artillery fired from the Ethiopian side began crossing the border and causing damage inside Kenya, we were displaced once again for a second time," he said. "In search of lasting safety, we left behind our home and property on the Ethiopian side of Moyale. After keeping my family in a temporary shelter for a while, I took them to Takaba Sub-County. Now, after getting my family to a safe place, I have returned to my home." Although he managed to move his family to a safer location, Abdi said the separation has compounded their hardship. His wife is now caring for their newborn without adequate support, while the family's business and source of income have effectively disappeared. "Moreover, my family is now separated; my wife has no one to help her where she is staying. The business we used to have is gone; we have no other income aside from what we spend out of our own pockets. If this continues, even if peace is restored in the future, our economy has been completely paralyzed," Abdi said. After taking my family to a secure place 200 kilometers away in Yabello, I returned to our neighborhood to protect my house from thieves and other threats Liban Guyo The conflict has also forced residents on the Oromia side to make difficult choices between protecting their families and safeguarding their homes and remaining property. Liban Guyo, another Moyale resident, told Addis Standard that he evacuated his family to Yabello, approximately 200 kilometers away, before returning alone to protect his property from looting and other threats. "After taking my family to a secure place 200 kilometers away in Yabello, I returned to our neighborhood to protect my house from thieves and other threats. Now that I am back, my house, where we used to hear the sound of children, has become completely empty," Liban told Addis Standard . He described a town whose ordinary rhythms of life have been replaced by an atmosphere of fear and militarization. "Our neighborhood has completely changed from what we used to know. Previously, when dawn broke in the morning, you would see children going to school and merchants arriving in town from various places. Now, none of that is visible; all we see are military forces." The deterioration becomes even more pronounced at night, when electricity outages and exchanges of heavy weapons have left residents facing prolonged darkness and insecurity. "In the evening, instead of electric lights, what your eyes see is heavy artillery fire being exchanged from both sides," he said. The accounts of Kule, Abdi and Liban illustrate different dimensions of the same crisis: families forced into repeated displacement, parents separated from their children and spouses, and residents returning to increasingly deserted neighborhoods to protect whatever remains of their livelihoods. Together, they reveal how the conflict is dismantling not only the physical security of Moyale's population but also the social and economic foundations of civilian life. A border economy brought to a standstill The humanitarian consequences are compounded by the disruption of economic activities that have historically sustained Moyale and surrounding communities. The town and the wider Borana borderlands depend heavily on pastoralism, livestock trading and cross-border commerce, with markets and commercial networks connecting communities on both sides of the Ethiopia-Kenya frontier. The fighting has brought livestock markets to a standstill, disrupted the movement of goods and left freight trucks stranded on both sides of the border. A November 11 Addis Standard analysis highlighted how the disruption has driven down livestock prices, undermining the livelihoods of pastoralist communities already exposed to economic and environmental pressures. The interruption of commercial trade has also contributed to shortages and rising prices of basic commodities, including cooking oil, rice and milk. This creates an additional burden for displaced families and host communities, particularly as humanitarian assistance struggles to keep pace with growing needs. The economic damage extends beyond the immediate loss of businesses and property. For pastoralist households, the inability to access markets can mean losing the principal source of income from livestock sales. For merchants, transporters and other small businesses, prolonged insecurity threatens commercial relationships and the capital accumulated over years of trading. Even if fighting subsides, restoring these economic networks will require more than the return of displaced residents. It will depend on the restoration of security, reopening of markets, resumption of cross-border movement and rebuilding of confidence among communities whose livelihoods have been severely disrupted. Kenya faces mounting pressure as violence crosses the border The deteriorating situation has increasingly become a concern for Kenyan authorities , as the conflict's humanitarian and security consequences extend beyond Ethiopia's territory. Professor Guyo Waqo, the Kenyan Member of Parliament representing the Kenyan side of Moyale, told Addis Standard that he was deeply concerned by the displacement of more than 50,000 Ethiopian citizens and the continued daily influx of refugees into Kenya. He said the Kenyan administration was coordinating with higher authorities to accommodate and assist displaced Ethiopians in locations including Oda, Olale, Somare, Al-Huda and Butiye. However, he warned that children and elderly people were particularly affected by shortages of milk and balanced nutrition. He also confirmed that several cases of diarrhea had been reported in the Oda area, which he attributed to rainfall and inadequate access to clean water, although no deaths had been recorded so far. Professor Guyo said he had raised the border crisis as an urgent matter in the Kenyan Parliament a week earlier, emphasizing the need for diplomatic engagement rather than allowing the conflict to further destabilize communities on both sides of the frontier. He acknowledged that the Kenyan government has limited authority to intervene directly in an internal conflict within Ethiopia. However, he said diplomatic pressure should be applied to encourage a resolution, alongside emergency assistance for those displaced by the fighting. The cross-border security implications have already become more serious. Professor Guyo said heavy weapons, including RPGs, fired from the Ethiopian side had killed two people and injured dozens inside Kenya, underscoring the danger of the conflict spilling further into Kenyan territory. The UK government has also warned its citizens against travelling to Moyale and within five kilometers of the border area, citing security concerns and the threat of attacks by Al-Shabaab. Kenyan authorities have deployed military forces to secure the border and prevent armed groups from entering their territory, Professor Guyo said, while reaffirming that Kenya remains prepared to receive Ethiopian refugees. Asked whether the displaced could eventually be relocated to established refugee camps such as Dadaab and Kakuma if the conflict persists, he said the proposal had not yet been discussed and would require consultations among relevant stakeholders. Professor Guyo also raised concerns about the political and ethnic rhetoric surrounding the conflict, alleging that some Kenyan politicians were contributing to tensions through inflammatory public statements. "Moyale town is Borana land; however, it is very suspicious that Kenyan officials and Members of Parliament of Somali descent, such as Ali Roba (Governor/Senator of Mandera) and Farah Maalim (MP for Garissa), are preaching hatred in the media and escalating rhetoric to displace the Borana people. These communities have fought each other for decades; what are they hoping for now?" said Professor Guyo. His remarks highlight that the risk that the ongoing fighting could intersect with existing tensions of ownership dispute in the wider border region, complicating efforts to contain the violence. A wider border insecurity beyond the Moyale conflict The risk of further destabilization is underscored by the overlapping security challenges confronting communities along the Ethiopia-Kenya border. On November 16, a separate attack in Ethiopia's Malkamari area killed at least six people, most of them women and children. Although Kenyan authorities clarified that the attack was unrelated to the Moyale conflict, media coverage and public discourse in Ethiopia have increasingly framed the incident as part of the wider conflict, potentially deepening tensions and reinforcing perceptions of an expanding cross-border confrontation. Kenyan authorities attributed the Malkamari attack to tensions involving the Garre and Degodia clans, stressing that it was distinct from the clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces in Moyale. They nevertheless noted that the perpetrators had taken advantage of the broader insecurity along the border. The distinction is important. While the Moyale conflict is rooted in territorial and political disputes involving regional forces, the wider border environment is characterized by overlapping security challenges, longstanding communal tensions and the movement of armed actors across difficult-to-police areas. The deterioration of security in one location can therefore create opportunities for violence elsewhere, even when the incidents have separate immediate causes. The conflict has also drawn increasing human rights scrutiny. On November 17, the Oromo Liberation Army criticized the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission for what it described as insufficient attention to civilian attacks and violence in areas including Moyale, while investigations have focused on other regions. The criticism adds to growing concerns about civilian protection and accountability as the conflict continues. The cost of a conflict without a political resolution Nearly a month into the fighting, Moyale's deteriorating situation raises broader questions about the ability of the federal government to contain regional disputes before they escalate into prolonged armed confrontations with devastating consequences for civilians. Since Monday, November 16, a third attempt to mediate between the warring factions has stalled, despite efforts involving local elders and federal government intervention, Addis Standard has learned. Meanwhile, the continued displacement of tens of thousands, destruction of homes and businesses, disruption of trade and increasing pressure on neighboring Kenya demonstrate that the consequences of the conflict are no longer confined to the immediate territorial dispute. The longer the fighting continues, the greater the likelihood that the humanitarian emergency will become entrenched and existing communal divisions will deepen. The accounts of residents also reveal the growing distance between the immediate security needs of civilians and the political and military dynamics sustaining the confrontation. While families seek safe shelter, food and the ability to resume ordinary life, neighborhoods remain deserted, businesses are shut and residents who return to protect their properties do so at considerable personal risk. For Kenya, the challenge is increasingly twofold: managing the humanitarian needs of a growing refugee population while preventing further violations of its territorial security. For Ethiopia, the continuing conflict presents an urgent civilian protection and governance challenge, with the need for political engagement becoming more pressing as the fighting spreads and the economic consequences widen. Residents and the Kenyan lawmaker interviewed by Addis Standard called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a lasting resolution through dialogue and diplomacy. For a town increasingly emptied of its civilians, the immediate question is no longer simply when residents can return home, but whether the security, economic and social conditions that once sustained their lives can be restored before the conflict leaves permanent scars on both sides of the border. ethiopia.summary: The escalating conflict in Moyale, Ethiopia, has led to a severe humanitarian crisis as clashes between Oromia and Somali regional forces have emptied the once-thriving border town of its civilian population. Since the conflict reignited on October 18, 2026, tens of thousands have fled to Kenya, with reports indicating that nearly 50,000 Ethiopians have crossed the border, exacerbating existing pressures on local resources. Displaced families face dire conditions, including food and water shortages, inadequate shelter, and disrupted education for children. The violence has also crippled the local economy, halting livestock trading and increasing prices for essential goods. Residents describe a town transformed from a vibrant community to a militarized zone, filled with fear and uncertainty. As the conflict continues, both Ethiopian and Kenyan authorities are struggling to address the growing humanitarian needs, highlighting the urgent requirement for international assistance and a resolution to restore peace and stability in the region.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Strengthened Defense Capacity Vital to National, Regional Security 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 18, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia’s growing defense capabilities are strengthening the country’s ability to safeguard its national interests and contribute to peace and stability across the region, Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Centre Gezahegn Fekadu said. Speaking exclusively to ENA, Gezahegn said the Ethiopian National Defense Force had significantly enhanced its operational capabilities through organizational reforms, improved weaponry, advanced training and broader capacity-building initiatives, particularly since the reform. He noted that the capabilities developed through domestic efforts had not only strengthened the country’s defense readiness but also enhanced its capacity to protect national interests and contribute to regional security. Gezahegn emphasized that sustaining these achievements requires continued military modernization to effectively respond to evolving security threats and challenges. He stressed that a capable and technologically advanced defense force is essential not only for safeguarding national interests but also for promoting regional stability and creating a peaceful environment in which countries can pursue their development objectives. He further noted that the capabilities built by the Defense Force, together with the sacrifices made in coordination with other security institutions, would play a significant role in protecting Ethiopia’s national interests and advancing peace and stability across the region. Meanwhile, Lieutenant Colonel Aragaw Gebremedhin, Policy and Strategy Affairs Team Leader at the Ethiopian National Defense College, said the Defense Force had continued to modernize in terms of technology, training and personnel strength. He noted that Ethiopia’s long-standing contribution to international peacekeeping, from Korea to various African countries, combined with its growing military capabilities, had strengthened its capacity to support peace and security domestically, in neighboring countries and beyond. Aragaw also called on universities and research institutions to document Ethiopia’s peacekeeping contributions and the development of its military capabilities through research and publications. Such efforts, he said, would help present Ethiopia’s peacekeeping experience and contributions more effectively to the international community. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

The decisions were made Thursday at a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre. Information Minister Abdulfatah Sheikh Abdulkadir announced the measures at a news conference following the meeting. The Cabinet instructed the Foreign Ministry to recall Somalia’s ambassador to the UAE for consultations and to inform the international community about what the government described as Emirati interference in Somalia’s internal affairs. The ministry accused Abu Dhabi of undermining Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. It maintained that the federal government is the country’s sole legally recognized authority responsible for conducting foreign relations. The ministry also rejected security agreements with foreign parties that are reached without the approval of the federal government. Diplomatic tensions between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi have intensified since January 2026, when Somalia’s Cabinet announced the cancellation of security, defense and economic cooperation agreements with the UAE. The dispute centers on allegations of Emirati interference in Somalia’s internal affairs, the UAE’s relations with regional administrations and security agreements it has entered into with parties in Somalia. The UAE has denied allegations of interference made by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. The initiative, dubbed Advocacy for Indebted Prisoners, was launched at a conference in Mogadishu on Thursday by the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs. The ministry said some inmates have completed the prison terms imposed by courts but remain in detention because they are unable to pay debts or financial compensation owed. According to figures presented at the conference, 292 inmates at Mogadishu's Central Prison are being held over debts or financial obligations, with a total outstanding amount of approximately $11.1 million. Of those, 188 are aged between 20 and 60, seven are elderly, 10 are women, and 35 are under the age of 20. The ministry also reported that 127 people were held over debts at the Central Prison during 2025 and 2026, although further details about that figure were not provided. Related articles Somalia and EU Discuss Security and Defence Cooperation in Brussels Jubaland President Inaugurates First Phase of Kismayo Port Modernisation Project The initiative aims to provide financial assistance to eligible prisoners from disadvantaged backgrounds who have served their sentences but remain incarcerated due to outstanding financial obligations. It does not cover inmates who are still serving prison sentences or those held over other charges unrelated to financial debts. The Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs says it will engage businesspeople, companies, financial institutions, charitable organisations, religious scholars and professional associations to mobilise funds to support eligible prisoners. The initiative will be led by Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Hassan Moalim, in collaboration with judicial institutions and prison administrations. A five-member committee will also be established to oversee and manage the donations collected under the initiative. The initiative comes amid overcrowding at Mogadishu's Central Prison. The facility was designed to accommodate 800 inmates but currently holds approximately 1,600 people, twice its intended capacity. somalia.content: As if the US-Iran War Wasn’t Chaotic Enough, Pirates Are Making a Comeback - Newsweek Poll Poll of the Day: Are Trump’s Friendly Relations With Xi Good or Bad for America? U.S. News Politics AI Politics Tech Fact Check Sports Global Iran War Russia-Ukraine Middle East China And Asia Live Blog Better Planet All World News Lifestyle Family & Parenting Entertainment Travel Pets Automotive Relationships Science Health Personal Finance Better Workplaces Readers Choice Opinion My Turn All Opinion Rankings Health Finance Products Education Workplaces Corporate Responsibility All Rankings Watch The 1600 The Royal Report Unconventional From The Paddock Newsmakers Extra Newsletters Dare to Dream Events Essays Podcasts Vantage Insights Magazine CEO Circle Announcements Leadership Dev Pragad Subscribe Sign In U.S. News Politics AI Politics Tech Fact Check Sports Global Iran War Russia-Ukraine Middle East China And Asia Live Blog Better Planet All World News Lifestyle Family & Parenting Entertainment Travel Pets Automotive Relationships Science Health Personal Finance Better Workplaces Readers Choice Opinion My Turn All Opinion Rankings Health Corporate Responsibility Finance Products Education Work All Rankings Watch The 1600 The Royal Report Unconventional From The Paddock Newsmakers Social Facebook Instagram YouTube Reddit TikTok Twitter/X Extra Newsletters Dare to Dream Events Essays Podcasts Vantage Insights Magazine CEO Circle Announcements Leadership Dev Pragad With international shipping already facing historic strains as a result of the crisis in the Middle East, one set of disruptors has found an opportunity to capitalize. Piracy off the coast of Somalia has surged to levels not seen since 2013. Hotspots include the very same waters that constitute a major theater of the U.S.-Iran war, in which Yemen's Tehran-aligned Ansar Allah movement, widely known as the Houthis, has targeted vessels from the other side of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, while the Islamic Republic wields leverage over the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint. Somali pirates don't appear to be taking sides, however. They've targeted vessels from the U.S., Iran and an array of other nations in what appears to be a comeback for a global challenge that once united the world's leading powers. "Somali piracy is an opportunistic crime," Ken Menkhaus, professor at Davidson College and former special political adviser in the U.N. Operation in Somalia, told Newsweek. "It flourished when piracy was low-risk, high-reward." "Right now, we've got a perfect storm of factors that are making it lower risk than it had been," he said. Problems from the Persian Gulf to Puntland One of the key factors Menkhaus identified as fueling the renewed Somali pirate threat was the diversion of naval forces toward addressing maritime threats directly linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict. "We've got naval patrols in the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean that are preoccupied with Houthi threats to shipping lanes in the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea, and as well in the Strait of Hormuz," Menkhaus said. "So, there's international inattention." At the same time, he pointed out that unrest in northeastern Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region that straddles the Horn of Africa is also contributing to the breakdown in order at sea. Local forces have been stretched thin between engaging in political clashes involving the central government and waging operations against the Somali wing of the Islamic State militant group, also known as ISIS-Somalia, or IS-Somalia. "The government in Mogadishu has deployed and recruited troops in Puntland, weakening Puntland’s maritime operations," Mohamed Daud Ismail, senior research assistant at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) monitor, told Newsweek. "Another reason is Puntland’s counter-insurgency operation targeting the Islamic State of Somalia Province in the mountainous ranges of the Bari region," Ismail said. "Puntland forces have focused more on operations against IS and on resolving disputes with the federal government. As a result, pirates have taken advantage of the security vacuum." The resulting intensification of Somali piracy, Ismail warned, could serve as "a severe force multiplier for the global maritime industry." "Because multinational naval coalitions are heavily committed to intercepting drone and missile threats in the Red Sea and managing escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz," he said, "reallocating surface combatants and patrol aircraft back across the vast Somali Basin creates dangerous security gaps in both theaters." Where Crises Converge The Gulf of Aden is not the only link between Somalia and Yemen. Ansar Allah, which now effectively controls the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait between the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea, has long been suspected of fostering tacit ties with armed non-state actors in Somalia. Among these groups is Al-Shabab. While the Al-Qaeda-affiliated organization's jihadi Sunni Islamist doctrine directly clashes with Ansar Allah's revolutionary Zaidi Shiite Muslim revivalist ideology, reports have identified some areas of common interest that may tie in the piracy problem as well. "The Houthis and Al-Shabab have also been linked to efforts to train and supply Somali pirates," Michael DeAngelo, Africa analyst at the American Enterprise Institute's Critical Threats Project, told Newsweek. "Al-Shabab has long-standing ties to piracy networks, and the Houthis may be leveraging their own growing ties to Al-Shabab to support the pirates in disrupting shipping through the Red Sea." Both factions thrive in chaos. And what DeAngelo described as a spike in "lucrative ransom payouts from hijackings" between 2024 and 2026 in the region may only serve to establish further grounds for collaboration. Meanwhile, Tehran may stand to benefit as well. Christopher Hockey, a Kenya-based senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, argued that "the real story right now is the convergence of threat actors in the Gulf of Aden, and the blurring of lines between conflicts in the Horn and those in the Arabian Peninsula—and potentially Iranian influence over it all." "Al-Shabab, the Houthis, Islamic State, organized criminals, and pirates are all operating in the Gulf of Aden, taking advantage of the same illicit networks—and driven by overlapping interests," Hockey told Newsweek. Even if the many other divergences in beliefs, objectives and tactics ultimately prevent any true coalescence among these actors, the result may prove the same. "Whether or not these relationships involve direct coordination is perhaps not significant," Hockey said. "Insecurity in the Gulf of Aden stretches the limited resources available to naval operations also trying to respond to Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and to the chaos in the Strait of Hormuz. " "Ultimately, Iran and its allies are able to disrupt maritime trade across a vast geography and through two of the world's most critical waterways," Hockey said. Short on Solutions Geopolitical tensions rocking the international order may also serve to prevent the kind of global unity that once helped put an end to the last Somali piracy epidemic. Beginning in late 2008 and expanding significantly in 2009, deteriorating maritime security conditions off Somalia prompted an unprecedented international counter-piracy effort, bringing together major powers, including the U.S., China and Russia. To this day, China, India, Japan, Russia and South Korea continue to deploy naval forces in the waters surrounding Somalia, while the European Union maintains its dedicated Operation Atalanta counter-piracy mission. The U.S. also participates in regional counter-piracy operations through Combined Task Force 151, part of the multinational Combined Maritime Forces. Yet Menkhaus was skeptical that the level partnership achieved in the past could be replicated in today's global security environment. "I think it's going to be much more difficult now, much more fraught," Menkhaus said. Rather, he predicted a response would involve greater reliance on armed private security contractors, a practice he credited with likely playing an even more effective role in deterring pirates in the past than warships. That doesn't mean hired guns will be enough to root out the problem today. Menkhaus identified a threefold combination of extreme poverty, poor governance and an entrenched culture of extracting tolls from land and sea routes that makes Somalia an especially attractive hub for pirates. Moreover, alternative sources of income are becoming more difficult to come by in Somalia. "The root causes of piracy in Somalia are primarily local factors related to illegal and unregulated fishing from foreign trawlers off the Somali coast that undermines local livelihoods," Omar Mahmood, senior analyst for Somalia and the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Newsweek. "While pirate groups feed off this dynamic, they are also fundamentally criminal actors that strike when they see opportunity," Mahmood said. The explosion of insecurity plaguing maritime passageways in the Middle East "provided precisely such an opportunity," he pointed out, with counter-piracy naval patrols redeployed north of Somalia and commercial traffic redirected south toward the pirates' hunting grounds. The result, he argued, "was more targets and less policing, giving the pirate groups an opportunity to revive their trade." Today, the scale of incidents remains far from their 2011 peak. Somali authorities and international partners have mobilized efforts to contain the outbreak. Even so, however, Mahmood predicted piracy would persist in the seas off Somalia. "We should expect episodic attacks to continue, in part because the criminal groups are not fully dismantled and the broader root causes around local fishing livelihoods remain unaddressed," Mahmood said. "Even small cycles of attack, however, can increase insurance premiums while pushing commercial traffic to take longer routes." "The net effect is to add costs to a shipping industry that is already reeling from restrictions from other crucial maritime passageways," he added. وصافة جدول الترتيب، ليصبح على مقربة من الصدارة في ظل أفضلية 3 مباريات مؤجلة، في وقت يواجه فيه مدربه جوزيف زينباور 3 تحديات صعبة أمام أحد أقوى أندية المنافسة. غيابات مؤثرة في صفوف الهلال السوداني ويخوض الهلال مباراته أمام منافسه الشرطة في ظل غيابات عديدة، إذ تسبب إرهاق لاعبي المنتخب بخوضهم سجالات عنيفة أمام المنتخب السنغالي، تخللتها رحلات شاقة، ووصولهم مؤخرًا من مدينة جوبا عاصمة جنوب السودان، في حرمان الفريق من جهود عدد منهم، مما يفتح الباب أمام ظهور عناصر جديدة يرغب المدرب في إعدادها للاستحقاقات القادمة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، حيث يستهل الفريق مشواره بمواجهة حوريا كوناكري الغيني يوم 29 نوفمبر الجاري على ملعب "أماهورو" بالعاصمة كيغالي. وغاب المدرب الألماني، الذي يقضي موسمه الأول مع النادي الأزرق، عن تدريبات الفريق لمدة 11 يومًا قضاها في بلاده خلال فترة التوقف الدولي، ولم يعد إلا قبل ساعات من مواجهة فريق الشرطة، مما اضطره للاعتماد على تقارير معاونيه لمتابعة سير الإعداد. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يتلقى دعما مزدوجا وزينباور يضع حدا للشائعات إدارة الهلال في مأزق محرج قبل تحديات محلية وقارية مهمة جاء ذلك في ظل تراجعٍ حاد في مستوى عناصره الأساسية التي شاركت مع المنتخب في تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية، وانهيارهم المعنوي عقب الهزائم القاسية التي تعرض لها "صقور الجديان" وتسببت في تضاؤل حظوظهم في بلوغ النهائيات، وهو ما يضع المدرب أمام تحدي إعادة الروح المعنوية للاعبيه الذين يشكلون قوام المنتخب وعموده الفقري. ويكثف مدرب الهلال السوداني جهوده لاستعادة توازن الفريق بعد تذبذب نتائجه في الدوري المحلي، ساعيًا لتصحيح المسار الفني وتجاوز مرحلة التراجع التي أدت إلى اهتزاز الثقة به، رغم نجاحه في تحقيق نتائج متميزة خلال المراحل التمهيدية للبطولة الأفريقية. وتبرز في الأفق (الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم) وسط حضور جماهيري كبير في ملعب «جذع النخلة» بالبصرة، خرج المنتخب العراقي بتعادل مثير أمام نظيره الإيراني بهدف لمثله، في ختام البطولة الرباعية الدولية التي تُوِّج بلقبها المنتخب الإيراني، في حين حلَّ أصحاب الأرض في المركز الثاني، في وقت فتحت فيه تصريحات رئيس الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم، يونس محمود، الباب أمام التساؤلات بشأن مستقبل المدرب الأسترالي غراهام أرنولد. وكان المنتخب العراقي قد تقدَّم بهدف مبكر سجَّله حسين علي في الدقيقة الأولى، قبل أن يدرك محمد أمين حزباوي التعادل للمنتخب الإيراني في الدقيقة 83، ليرفع الأخير رصيده إلى 4 نقاط ويُتوَّج باللقب، مقابل نقطتين للعراق، الذي سبق أن تعادل مع لبنان في افتتاح البطولة. وتزامنت هذه النتائج مع تقدم المنتخب العراقي مركزاً واحداً في التصنيف الجديد للاتحاد الدولي لكرة القدم (فيفا)، ليحتل المرتبة 62 عالمياً والسادسة آسيوياً، برصيد 1400.66 نقطة. وأبدى أرنولد رضاه عن أداء لاعبيه أمام إيران، مؤكداً أن المنتخب العراقي أثبت قدرته على منافسة أحد أفضل 4 منتخبات في القارة الآسيوية، رغم مشاركة عدد من اللاعبين الشباب الذين لم يخوضوا تحت قيادته سوى حصتين تدريبيَّتين. وقال المدرب الأسترالي، خلال المؤتمر الصحافي عقب المباراة، إن لاعبيه قدَّموا أداءً جيداً أمام منتخب إيراني قوي، وكانوا الأقرب لتحقيق الفوز، مشيراً إلى أن منح الفرصة للعناصر الشابة يمثل جزءاً أساسياً من المشروع الفني الذي يعمل عليه. وشدَّد أرنولد على أن بناء منتخب قادر على مقارعة كبار آسيا يتطلب عملاً يتجاوز مجرد استدعاء اللاعبين إلى المنتخب الأول، موضحاً أن الاستثمار الحقيقي يجب أن يبدأ من منتخبات الفئات العمرية، وفق معايير وأهداف واضحة. وأضاف أن رئيس الاتحاد طلب بناء منتخب للمستقبل، وأن العودة إلى منافسة كبار القارة تتطلب الاهتمام بتطوير اللاعبين الشباب، خصوصاً منتخب تحت 23 عاماً، والعمل على التأهل إلى الألعاب الأولمبية. إيران توجت بالكأس بعد تصدرها فرق البطولة (الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم) واستشهد أرنولد بتجربته السابقة مع المنتخب الأسترالي، وكذلك بتجربة الكرة العراقية مطلع الألفية، عندما تأهل المنتخب الأولمبي إلى «أولمبياد أثينا 2004»، قبل أن يتوَّج المنتخب الأول بلقب كأس آسيا، عاداً أن الاستثمار في الفئات العمرية يمثل الطريق الصحيح لبناء منتخب قوي ومستدام. وفي تشخيصه لأبرز المشكلات الفنية، كشف المدرب الأسترالي عن تقديم تقرير يتعلق بأزمة مركز المهاجم الصريح «رقم 9» في المسابقة المحلية، موضحاً أنه لا يجد مهاجماً محلياً جاهزاً للاختيار، في ظلِّ عدم اكتمال الجاهزية البدنية لميمي، وإصابة علي الحمادي. وأشاد أرنولد بإمكانات اللاعب الشاب أموري فيصل، وكذلك بالمستوى الذي قدَّمه الحارس كميل خلال مباراتين، لكنه أشار إلى أن قلة مشاركة بعض اللاعبين مع أنديتهم تمثل تحدياً أمام الجهاز الفني، خصوصاً فيما يتعلق بجاهزيتهم البدنية للمباريات الدولية. وتطرق إلى وضع حيدر عبد الكريم، مؤكداً أن اللاعب مطالب بمعالجة وضعه بنفسه، بعدما ابتعد عن المشاركة لمدة عامين، مشيراً إلى أن حيدر وداريو نامو لا يشاركان مع نادييهما، وأن اللاعب الذي ينضم إلى المنتخب يجب أن يكون جاهزاً لخوض المباريات الدولية. بدوره، أثار رئيس الاتحاد العراقي لكرة القدم يونس محمود، التساؤلات بشأن هوية المدرب الذي سيقود المرحلة المقبلة، بعدما أكد أن خيار المدرب المحلي مستبعد من حسابات الاتحاد. وأوضح محمود، في تصريحات نقلتها «وكالة الأنباء العراقية»، أن الاتحاد يبحث عن مدرب من خارج العراق يمتلك القدرة على التعامل مع عقليات اللاعبين المحترفين في الدوريات الأوروبية، مشيراً إلى وجود 15 لاعباً عراقياً ينشطون في أوروبا. وقال إن الاتحاد لا يريد تكرار الأخطاء السابقة في اختيار المدربين، بعدما شهد هذا الملف كثيراً من الجدل، مؤكداً أهمية الوصول إلى توليفة متجانسة يكون فيها اللاعبون مكملين لبعضهم بعضاً. وأشار رئيس الاتحاد إلى أن المدرب القادم قد يكون أرنولد نفسه أو غيره، وأن المعيار الأساسي في الاختيار سيكون القدرة على التعامل مع اللاعبين المحترفين في أوروبا وفهم طبيعة عقلياتهم. مواضيع رياضة كرة القدم العراق عودة الدوليين تشعل تدريبات الأهلي المصري قبل 2027، بفوزه 4ـ2 على مضيفه السوداني، في مباراة جمعتهما، الإثنين، على ملعب مدينة جوبا، عاصمة جنوب السودان، لحساب الجولة الرابعة من عاشر مجموعات التصفيات. وجلس الثلاثي السنغالي خاليدو كوليبالي، مدافع الهلال، وموري دياو، حارس مرمى الشباب، وكلايتون دياندي، جناح الدرعية، على مقاعد البدلاء دون مشاركة، فيما لعب مواطنهم مالانج سار، مدافع نيوم، المباراة كاملة، ودخل زميلهم ديون لوبي، لاعب وسط الاتحاد، بديلًا في الدقيقة 77، وصنع الهدف الثالث بتمريرة طويلة. وتقدم السنغاليون بهدفين سجلهما نيكولاس جاكسون، رأس الحربة، والحاج مالك ضيوف، الظهير الأيسر، في الدقيقتين 4 و22. واستطاع السودان إدراك التعادل عن طريق الجزولي نوح، وصلاح الدين عادل، لاعبي الوسط، في الدقيقتين 52 و75. وفيما كان المنتخب السوداني يبحث عن إكمال العودة والفوز، تلقت شباكه هدفًا سنغاليًا في الدقيقة 87 بتوقيع الجناح باتي مبوب، وتبعه آخر بواسطة المهاجم بول ميندي مع بداية الوقت بدل الضائع، ليحسم «أسود التيرانجا» اللقاء. وتجبر الظروف الراهنة في السودان المنتخب الملقب بـ «صقور الجديان» على اللعب خارج أرضه في مدينة جوبا. ورفع الفوز رصيد السنغال إلى 10 نقاط، وواصلت احتلال الصدارة، أمام موزمبيق صاحبة النقاط الأربع، والسودان وإثيوبيا المتساويتين بثلاث نقاط. وتتواجه موزمبيق مع إثيوبيا، الثلاثاء، لحساب الجولة ذاتها في محاولة لتعزيز football.summary: أمجد قلق هو مهاجم نادي الهلال السوداني، يحمل القميص رقم 36، ويبلغ من العمر 23 عامًا، حيث وُلد في 1 نوفمبر 2003. يُعتبر قلق من اللاعبين البارزين في الفريق، ويشارك في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. الهلال السوداني لديه عدة مباريات قادمة في مرحلة المجموعات، حيث سيواجه فريق هورويا في 29 نوفمبر 2026، ثم المغرب الفاسي في 4 ديسمبر 2026، وبيراميدز في 18 ديسمبر 2026. كما سيستمر الفريق في المنافسة مع هورويا مرة أخرى في 15 يناير 2027، ويختتم مبارياته في هذه المرحلة بمواجهة المغرب الفاسي في 22 يناير 2027. يُعتبر الهلال السوداني من الأندية العريقة في كرة القدم الأفريقية، ويطمح لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في البطولات القادمة. لمزيد من المعلومات حول اللاعب وأخباره، يمكن الاشتراك في النشرة البريدية لمتابعة آخر المستجدات.
